title: We Bulldozed the Ecosystem of Childhood Then Blamed Kids For Struggling
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Kevin Stinehart uses the metaphor of an ecological habitat to diagnose the current crisis in child development: just as deer began eating his school garden after nearby forests were cleared for development, children are showing up in schools behaviourally and emotionally underprepared because society has systematically cleared the natural habitat in which childhood development occurs. The essay catalogues what was removed -- unstructured free play, neighbourhood packs of children, walks to school, boredom, small risks, petty arguments to solve alone, mixed-age groups, and the chance to be annoying and discover social consequences without adult mediation. Stinehart's central word is 'reps': each of these experiences provided children with repetitions in frustration tolerance, social courage, conflict navigation, independence, and executive function. When the habitat was cleared -- gradually, with individually-reasonable justifications like safety, convenience, and academic pressure -- the reps disappeared, and children now arrive at school lacking capacities that prior generations developed incidentally through daily life. Adults then blame children for the deficit rather than recognising the structural cause. Schools respond with elaborate downstream systems that help individuals but do not restore the ecosystem. The prescription is honest diagnosis: children need conditions that give them room to become capable, and adults need to start rebuilding the forest instead of perfecting the fence.
points: * The 'reps' framing reframes behavioural and developmental problems not as character deficits but as training deficits: children lack competencies they used to develop through accumulated incidental practice in childhood's natural habitat. * Adults have created an environment where every hour is scheduled, every conflict mediated, every risk softened, and every boredom treated as a problem -- then are surprised when children cannot self-regulate or resolve conflict without help. * Downstream intervention systems (charts, calming corners, social-skills curricula) address the symptom of an individual child, not the structural cause -- like building a better fence while the forest stays cleared. * The individually-reasonable decisions that cleared the childhood habitat -- safety, convenience, liability, busy schedules, academic pressure, screens -- collectively produced an outcome none of the individual decisions intended. * The question adults should ask is not 'what is wrong with kids these days?' but 'what happened to the healthy childhood ecosystem they were supposed to grow in?' -- which shifts responsibility from the child to the environment.
quotes: We have cleared away so much of the natural habitat children used to grow inside. Not cruelly. Not usually on purpose. Most of the time, we had reasons that made sense in the moment. Safety. Convenience. Busy schedules. Academic pressure. Liability. But little by little, we cleared the natural habitat of childhood.
Then children show up in school hungry for the exact capacities a healthy childhood habitat used to give them, and we blame the kids for not having them.

A child used to practice frustration tolerance by losing a backyard game and having to keep playing because going inside meant there was nothing to do except stare at wallpaper and reconsider your life choices.

We took away the reps the childhood ecosystem provided. Then we got surprised when children looked underdeveloped. We started lifting the weight for the child each time a struggle came up then wondered why they were so weak in self-regulation, executive function, interpersonal skills, and self-direction.
A support is not the same thing as an ecosystem. A deer eating my school garden may need a better fence. But the fence does not explain why the deer are suddenly there more often.

Because children are not supposed to grow up inside a world where every hour is scheduled, every conflict is mediated, every risk is softened, every silence is filled, every boredom is treated as a problem, every movement is contained, and every social experience is either adult-run or screen-based.
And when children do not get enough room to become capable, their needs do not disappear. They just show up somewhere. Usually in the least convenient place possible.
